extracted.intended_audience: general readers, comedians, comedy scholars, and students of humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for creating or identifying anti-humor (anti-jokes / anti-comedy): humor that relies on absence or reversal of an expected punchline, various subtypes, and performance techniques used in stand-up contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of expected punchline / surprise from lack
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor is based on the surprise factor of absence of an expected joke or of a punch line in a narration that is set up as a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humor arises from the anticlimax created when the listener's expectation of a conventional punchline is deliberately subverted or denied. This is the core defining feature: set up like a joke, but the expected payoff is missing or withheld, producing a comedic effect for some audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticlimax realized as the shaggy dog story (the yarn)
rubrics_metrics.description: The yarn, or shaggy dog story, is a type of anti-humor involving telling an extremely long joke with an intricate (sometimes grisly) back story and surreal or repetitive plotline before ending with either a weak spoonerism, abruptly stopping with no real punchline at all, or using a 'no soap radio' style ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prolonged, detailed buildup and deliberately underwhelming or non-existent resolution to create the anticlimax. The length and excessive detail are part of the technique; the payoff is intentionally weak or absent to produce the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious punchline (anti-humor via banality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some anti-humor uses a structure like a traditional joke (set-up and punchline) but makes the punchline the most obvious or banal response to the set-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'Why did the chicken cross the road?' or farmer jokes where the answer is literally restating the obvious (e.g., 'Where's my tractor?'). The comedic device is that the 'punchline' is expected and mundane rather than surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provokes emotions opposite to traditional humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor can be described as a form of irony or reversal of expectations that may provoke emotions opposite to humor, such as fear, pain, embarrassment, disgust, awkwardness, or discomfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators may intentionally aim for discomfort or awkwardness rather than laughter. Recognize that the intended effect can be non-laughter responses; effectiveness depends on audience and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of the traditional joke (role within alternative comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor is often a component of alternative comedy and parodies the traditional idea of the joke as a form of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anti-humor to critique or subvert joke conventions. In alternative comedy contexts, anti-humor may serve broader artistic or satirical purposes rather than merely eliciting laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately bad stand-up and performance-persona techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor in stand-up is associated with deliberately bad comedians or performance art personas who use untalented or awkward presentation as part of the comic effect (e.g., Andy Kaufman's Tony Clifton persona).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include adopting an untalented or obnoxious persona, using quasi-surreal acts, or intentionally failing comedic expectations. Historical examples: Andy Kaufman's performance art and persona Tony Clifton; Norm Macdonald is sometimes associated with anti-humor performances (though he disputed the label).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non sequitur / nonsense devices (e.g., 'no soap radio')
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor can employ nonsense phrases or non sequitur devices (such as 'no soap radio') as endings that provide no logical or conventional punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices rely on absurdity or complete lack of resolution; they function by refusing to give a conventional semantic payoff, thereby producing surprise, confusion, or discomfort as the 'humorous' element.
